transcript.text: Every so often when I put the washing machine on the whole kitchen power goes off and I have to go to the fuse box and flick the switch back up. It doesn't happen every time. Indesit, IWE 7 something.

This is a common problem and usually fixable. The washing machine is most likely leaking a small amount of current to earth, and your **RCD** (the safety switch in the fuse box) is cutting the power to protect you.

## First, check which switch is tripping

In your fuse box, look at the switch that flicks down:

- **A wider switch, often labelled "RCD" or with a "T"/test button**, which cuts power to several circuits. This is an **earth leakage** trip and the most likely cause.
- **A narrower switch for just the kitchen circuit (an MCB)**. This means **too much current** or a short circuit. It's less common with washing machines, but it can happen if the machine runs alongside a kettle, oven, or tumble dryer on the same circuit.

## Likely causes (for an RCD trip), most common first

1. **Faulty heating element.** This is by far the most common cause on Indesits. As the element ages, its insulation breaks down and leaks current to earth, often only once it's hot or wet. That explains why it doesn't happen every time.
2. **Water leak inside the machine** dripping onto the motor, wiring, or element. Look for damp or rust underneath or inside the back panel.
3. **Motor or suppressor (interference filter)** breaking down.
4. **Cumulative leakage.** Several appliances on the same RCD each leak a little (fridge, freezer, etc.), and the washing machine tips it over the limit. This is more likely in older fuse boxes with one RCD covering lots of circuits.

## Simple tests you can do

- **Note *when* it trips.** Does it trip at the very start, a few minutes in when heating, during a fast spin, or when draining? Heating-stage trips point strongly at the element.
- **Run a cold wash (20°C or "cold").** If it never trips on cold but sometimes does on 40°C or higher, the element is the prime suspect.
- **Try it on a different socket or circuit** if you can reach one with the machine (not with a cheap extension lead). If it still trips, the fault is in the machine. If it doesn't, the issue may be the kitchen circuit or cumulative leakage.
- **Check the plug and socket** for scorch marks, looseness, or water nearby.

## Fixing it

- An **Indesit IWE7 heating element** typically costs around £15–30 and is a fairly common DIY job: unplug the machine, remove the back panel, and the element sits under the drum. Search for "Indesit IWE7 heater replacement" plus your full model number, which is on the sticker inside the door rim.
- An **appliance repairer or electrician** can do an **insulation resistance test** on the machine in a few minutes, which pinpoints whether the element, motor, or something else is leaking.
- If the machine is old and also has a bad leak or a worn drum bearing, replacing it may be better value than repairing it.

## Safety

- Unplug the machine before opening or inspecting it.
- **Don't** swap it onto a socket without RCD protection to "stop the tripping." The RCD is doing its job, and an earth fault on a metal-cased, wet appliance is genuinely dangerous.
- If the RCD trips even with the washing machine unplugged, call an electrician, because the fault is elsewhere.

If you tell me at what stage of the cycle it trips and which switch goes, I can narrow it down further.

Thanks, that's useful. I've kept notes on this: it's the RCD switch for the kitchen ring that goes, not one of the small individual breakers. It only happens a few minutes into 40 or 60 degree washes, never on cold, quick 30 or rinse and spin. It's been roughly 1 in 4 washes over the last month, and I've been resetting it each time. I tried the machine in a hall socket and it tripped that RCD once too. The plug looks fine, not warm and no marks. The door label says IWE 71451 B ECO UK.

Your notes make this pretty clear: **it's almost certainly the heating element.**

- It trips only on 40/60° washes, a few minutes in. That's exactly when the element switches on, and a quick 30 often barely uses it.
- It never trips on cold or rinse and spin, when the element isn't powered.
- It tripped the hall RCD too, so the fault is in the machine, not the kitchen wiring.
- It's intermittent because the leakage gets worse as the element heats and gets wet, so it sometimes stays just under the RCD's trip threshold.

## In the meantime

- **Stick to cold or quick-30 washes** until it's fixed, and stop resetting it on heated washes. The RCD is protecting you from a real fault, and repeated earth faults can get worse.
- Don't run it on any socket that isn't RCD-protected.

## The part

Search for **"Indesit IWE 71451 heating element"** or enter the full model on a parts site (eSpares, Partmaster, Buy Spares, or Indesit's own site). Then:

- **Match by model number, not by photo.** Indesits of this era use a few similar-looking elements, usually 1700–1800W.
- Check whether the **temperature sensor (NTC)** comes fitted. On many of these it clips into the element. If yours doesn't include one, you can move the old one across.
- Expect to pay around **£15–35**.

## Fitting it (about 30–60 minutes)

1. **Unplug the machine** and turn off the water taps. Have towels ready, as a little water may come out.
2. Pull the machine out and **remove the back panel** (a few screws).
3. The element is at the **bottom of the drum tub**, with wires attached and a nut in the middle.
4. **Take a photo of the wiring**, then pull off the connectors and the sensor.
5. **Loosen the centre nut** a few turns, push the bolt in to release the rubber seal, then wiggle the element out.
6. Slide the new one in. Make sure it **sits in the bracket at the back of the tub**, which you can feel or see with a torch. If it misses the bracket, it can touch the drum.
7. Tighten the nut firmly but not excessively, refit the wires and sensor exactly as in your photo, and refit the panel.
8. Run a **60° wash and watch for leaks** around the element seal.

YouTube has plenty of videos for "Indesit IWE heating element replacement" that show these exact steps.

## If you'd rather not DIY

A local appliance repairer can confirm it with an insulation test and swap it in one visit, typically £60–100 including the part.

If it still trips after a new element on a heated wash, the next suspects are a water leak onto the element wiring or the wiring loom itself. But given your pattern, I'd be surprised if it doesn't fix it.
